articles.title: Afghanistan: Asia and the Pacific: Weekly Regional Humanitarian Snapshot (14 - 20 July 2026)
articles.description: Countries: Afghanistan, Myanmar Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached Infographic. MYANMAR In Myanmar, monsoon-related flooding has affected communities across several states, causing displacement and damage to homes and livelihoods. In Rakhine State, heavy rainfall and rising river levels since early July have affected at least 10 of 17 townships, impacting nearly 100,000 people and damaging homes, household assets, livelihoods and paddy fields. While floodwaters have reportedly receded in some areas and people who temporarily evacuated have returned home, many households face urgent humanitarian needs and reduced recovery capacity. In Kachin State, flooding triggered by heavy rainfall since 17 July has affected Hpakant, Myitkyina and Waingmaw townships, including displacement sites hosting vulnerable communities. At least 500 displaced people were affected, although the full extent of impacts remains unclear in some locations due to communication challenges. Local communities, humanitarian partners and authorities are supporting response efforts. The flooding underscores the growing impact of climate-related shocks on already vulnerable communities and highlights the importance of timely, flexible resources for preparedness, anticipatory action and early recovery, particularly as humanitarian needs continue to outpace available funding. Source: UN, partner AFGHANISTAN On 20 July, heavy rainfall and flash floods affected parts of eastern Afghanistan, with the most severe impact reported in Parun City, Nuristan Province. As of 21 July, preliminary assessments indicated that at least 23 people have been killed and 15 were injured, while search and rescue operations continued and the number of missing persons remained unknown. In Parun, 22 houses were destroyed and 45 severely damaged, while five markets and some 70 local shops were also damaged. Four bridges, six road sections, protection walls, irrigation infrastructure and a water-supply network serving approximately 1,000 families were also affected. Around 50 jeribs (10 hectares) of agricultural land were impacted. In Nangarhar Province, three Afghan refugees were reportedly killed and nine injured at a returnee transit camp on the Pakistani side of the border. In Alingar District, Laghman Province, agricultural land and irrigation systems were affected, with no residential damage reported as of 21 July. Search and rescue operations and initial humanitarian response activities are ongoing in the affected areas. Immediate needs include emergency shelter, food, health and medical supplies, non-food items, safe drinking water and mental health and psychosocial support.

articles.title: Satellite images show Iran rebuilding fast despite US Israeli strikes
articles.description: The reporting suggests Iran's military infrastructure is proving more resilient than the US and Israeli campaigns intended, which cuts against the narrative of a decisively weakened Tehran. For oil markets already pricing supply risk from the Strait of Hormuz and now the Red Sea, evidence that Iran retains missile production know-how and repair capacity argues against any near term de-escalation. If Iran's capacity to strike shipping and regional targets is more durable than assumed, the current risk premium in crude may prove sticky rather than transient, and traders are likely to stay cautious on any dips tied to hopes of a swift resolution. --- Iran is rebuilding faster than expected, undercutting claims that the air campaign delivered a knockout blow. Summary: Satellite images from Planet Labs and Airbus show Iran repairing missile bases, a bridge and a Caspian shipyard within weeks of strikes Israeli officials say strikes often only collapsed tunnel entrances at mountain missile bases, leaving weapons stored inside intact Iran has continued precise strikes on ships and missile attacks on US allies Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan, including one that killed three US soldiers A former Israeli air and missile defense commander said Iran previously showed strong industrial rebuilding capacity after the 2025 12-day war Some analysts say Iran may have stockpiled advanced components, such as carbon fiber parts, allowing short-term missile assembly even as full reconstruction of some facilities could take years The White House maintains the campaign was a resounding victory, saying it destroyed Iran's missile arsenal and production and sank its navy Iran has rapidly rebuilt infrastructure hit by months of US and Israeli airstrikes, according to the Wall Street Journal (gated ), citing satellite imagery and Israeli and Western officials. Repairs have been documented at missile bases near Kangavar, Dezful and Kermanshah, a bombed bridge fixed within days, and partial reconstruction at a Caspian Sea shipyard linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Israeli officials told the Journal that strikes frequently only collapsed tunnel entrances at mountain missile bases rather than destroying the sites, leaving stored weapons intact for Iran to later dig out. Despite more than 20,000 strikes at the campaign's height, Iran has kept landing precise hits on shipping and striking US allies including Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan. The pace of recovery is prompting private frustration among Israeli officials, with one telling the Journal "Iran is rebuilding everything" and expressing concern about the trajectory. Analysts note some advanced components could take years to replace, but stockpiled parts may allow shorter-term missile assembly. The White House maintains the campaign was a decisive success, saying it dismantled Iran's missile production and naval capability. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Honduras - Operational update - June 2026
articles.description: Country: Honduras Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. Context June was marked by continued violence, insecurity, forced displacement risks and legal developments affecting the protection environment in Honduras. Reports during the month highlighted the persistence of organized criminal activity, extortion, violence against women, land-related conflicts, risks affecting children and adolescents, and climate-related pressures on communities with limited livelihood opportunities. Forced displacement remained a key concern. The Norwegian Refugee Council ranked Honduras among the world's ten most neglected displacement crises, citing limited international attention, insufficient humanitarian funding and reduced political engagement. National human rights institutions also warned that violence continues to drive displacement, with many families facing insecurity and limited access to protection before leaving their communities or the country. Violence continued to affect community safety and mobility. The Violence Observatory of the National Autonomous University of Honduras reported that some smaller municipalities are recording higher homicide rates than major urban centres, linking these trends to the expansion of organized crime and drug trafficking outside the country's largest cities. Authorities also reported increasingly fragmented extortion dynamics, with independent criminal actors accounting for a large share of complaints in recent years. Women, children and adolescents remained exposed to heightened protection risks. Civil society organizations reported at least 135 femicides so far in 2026, while child protection actors documented a 12 per cent increase in violent deaths of children, adolescents and young people compared to the same period in 2025. During the reporting period, the National Congress approved legal reforms to increase penalties for femicide and strengthen sanctions under the Law against Domestic Violence. The National Congress approved the Agro-industrial, Energy and Tourism Promotion Law and related reforms regulating evictions from occupied agricultural land. Indigenous, campesino and human rights organizations expressed concerns that the measures could increase risks of criminalization, displacement and tensions around longstanding land disputes. Climate-related shocks added pressure to communities already affected by violence. National authorities warned that a prolonged dry spell could reduce basic grain production and affect food security for thousands of families. In southern Honduras, coastal communities in Cedeño, experienced impacts from storm surges associated with Tropical Storm Cristina, while human rights organizations called for a rights-based approach to the planned relocation of Cedeño.
